This list includes all events which have been classified as [genocide](/wiki/Genocide "Genocide") by significant scholarship. As there are varying [definitions of genocide](/wiki/Definitions_of_genocide "Definitions of genocide"), this list includes events around which there is ongoing scholarly debate over their classification as *genocide* and is not a list of only events which have a scholarly consensus to recognize them as genocide. This list excludes [mass killings](/wiki/Mass_killing "Mass killing") which have not been explicitly defined as genocidal.[[a]](#cite_note-2)

Definitions
-----------

Main article: [Genocide definitions](/wiki/Genocide_definitions "Genocide definitions")

Scholarship varies on the [definition of genocide](/wiki/Genocide_definitions "Genocide definitions") employed when analysing whether events are genocidal in nature.[[2]](#cite_note-3) The United Nations [Genocide Convention](/wiki/Genocide_Convention "Genocide Convention"), not always employed, defines genocide as "any of the following acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group, as such: killing members of the group; causing serious bodily or mental harm to members of the group; deliberately inflicting on the group conditions of life calculated to bring about its physical destruction in whole or in part; imposing measures intended to prevent births within the group; [and] forcibly transferring children of the group to another group".[[3]](#cite_note-4) This and other definitions are generally regarded by the majority of genocide scholars to have an "[intent to destroy](/wiki/Genocidal_intent "Genocidal intent")" as a requirement for any act to be labelled genocide; there is also growing agreement on the inclusion of the physical destruction criterion.[[4]](#cite_note-AdamJones2024-5) Writing in 1998, professors of sociology Kurt Jonassohn and Karin Björnson stated that the Genocide Convention was a legal instrument resulting from a diplomatic compromise; the wording of the treaty is not intended to be a definition suitable as a research tool, and although it is used for this purpose, as it has an international legal credibility that others lack, other definitions have also been postulated. Jonassohn and Björnson go on to say that for various reasons, none of these alternative definitions have gained widespread support.[[5]](#cite_note-6)

Three genocides in history have been recognized under the 1948 legal definition: the [Cambodian genocide](/wiki/Cambodian_genocide "Cambodian genocide"), the [Rwandan genocide](/wiki/Rwandan_genocide "Rwandan genocide"), and the [Srebrenica massacre](/wiki/Srebrenica_massacre "Srebrenica massacre").[[6]](#cite_note-Samuel_2023-7)

According to Ernesto Verdeja, associate professor of political science and peace studies at the University of Notre Dame, there are three ways to conceptualize genocide other than the legal definition: in academic social science, in international politics and policy, and in colloquial public usage. The academic social science approach does not require proof of intent,[[6]](#cite_note-Samuel_2023-7) and social scientists often define genocide more broadly.[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurga2023-8) The international politics and policy definition centres around prevention policy and intervention and may actually mean "large-scale violence against civilians" when used by governments and international organizations. Lastly, Verdeja says the way the general public colloquially uses "genocide" is usually "as a stand-in term for the greatest evils".[[6]](#cite_note-Samuel_2023-7)

This list includes all events which have been classified as [genocide](/wiki/Genocide "Genocide") by significant scholarship. As there are varying [definitions of genocide](/wiki/Definitions_of_genocide "Definitions of genocide"), this list includes events around which there is ongoing scholarly debate over their classification as *genocide* and is not a list of only events which have a scholarly consensus to recognize them as genocide. This list excludes [mass killings](/wiki/Mass_killing "Mass killing") which have not been explicitly defined as genocidal.[[a]](#cite_note-2)

Definitions
-----------

Main article: [Genocide definitions](/wiki/Genocide_definitions "Genocide definitions")

Scholarship varies on the [definition of genocide](/wiki/Genocide_definitions "Genocide definitions") employed when analysing whether events are genocidal in nature.[[2]](#cite_note-3) The United Nations [Genocide Convention](/wiki/Genocide_Convention "Genocide Convention"), not always employed, defines genocide as "any of the following acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group, as such: killing members of the group; causing serious bodily or mental harm to members of the group; deliberately inflicting on the group conditions of life calculated to bring about its physical destruction in whole or in part; imposing measures intended to prevent births within the group; [and] forcibly transferring children of the group to another group".[[3]](#cite_note-4) This and other definitions are generally regarded by the majority of genocide scholars to have an "[intent to destroy](/wiki/Genocidal_intent "Genocidal intent")" as a requirement for any act to be labelled genocide; there is also growing agreement on the inclusion of the physical destruction criterion.[[4]](#cite_note-AdamJones2024-5) Writing in 1998, professors of sociology Kurt Jonassohn and Karin Björnson stated that the Genocide Convention was a legal instrument resulting from a diplomatic compromise; the wording of the treaty is not intended to be a definition suitable as a research tool, and although it is used for this purpose, as it has an international legal credibility that others lack, other definitions have also been postulated. Jonassohn and Björnson go on to say that for various reasons, none of these alternative definitions have gained widespread support.[[5]](#cite_note-6)

Three genocides in history have been recognized under the 1948 legal definition: the [Cambodian genocide](/wiki/Cambodian_genocide "Cambodian genocide"), the [Rwandan genocide](/wiki/Rwandan_genocide "Rwandan genocide"), and the [Srebrenica massacre](/wiki/Srebrenica_massacre "Srebrenica massacre").[[6]](#cite_note-Samuel_2023-7)

According to Ernesto Verdeja, associate professor of political science and peace studies at the University of Notre Dame, there are three ways to conceptualize genocide other than the legal definition: in academic social science, in international politics and policy, and in colloquial public usage. The academic social science approach does not require proof of intent,[[6]](#cite_note-Samuel_2023-7) and social scientists often define genocide more broadly.[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurga2023-8) The international politics and policy definition centres around prevention policy and intervention and may actually mean "large-scale violence against civilians" when used by governments and international organizations. Lastly, Verdeja says the way the general public colloquially uses "genocide" is usually "as a stand-in term for the greatest evils".[[6]](#cite_note-Samuel_2023-7)

This list includes all events which have been classified as [genocide](/wiki/Genocide "Genocide") by significant scholarship. As there are varying [definitions of genocide](/wiki/Definitions_of_genocide "Definitions of genocide"), this list includes events around which there is ongoing scholarly debate over their classification as *genocide* and is not a list of only events which have a scholarly consensus to recognize them as genocide. This list excludes [mass killings](/wiki/Mass_killing "Mass killing") which have not been explicitly defined as genocidal.[[a]](#cite_note-2)

Definitions
-----------

Main article: [Genocide definitions](/wiki/Genocide_definitions "Genocide definitions")

Scholarship varies on the [definition of genocide](/wiki/Genocide_definitions "Genocide definitions") employed when analysing whether events are genocidal in nature.[[2]](#cite_note-3) The United Nations [Genocide Convention](/wiki/Genocide_Convention "Genocide Convention"), not always employed, defines genocide as "any of the following acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group, as such: killing members of the group; causing serious bodily or mental harm to members of the group; deliberately inflicting on the group conditions of life calculated to bring about its physical destruction in whole or in part; imposing measures intended to prevent births within the group; [and] forcibly transferring children of the group to another group".[[3]](#cite_note-4) This and other definitions are generally regarded by the majority of genocide scholars to have an "[intent to destroy](/wiki/Genocidal_intent "Genocidal intent")" as a requirement for any act to be labelled genocide; there is also growing agreement on the inclusion of the physical destruction criterion.[[4]](#cite_note-AdamJones2024-5) Writing in 1998, professors of sociology Kurt Jonassohn and Karin Björnson stated that the Genocide Convention was a legal instrument resulting from a diplomatic compromise; the wording of the treaty is not intended to be a definition suitable as a research tool, and although it is used for this purpose, as it has an international legal credibility that others lack, other definitions have also been postulated. Jonassohn and Björnson go on to say that for various reasons, none of these alternative definitions have gained widespread support.[[5]](#cite_note-6)

Three genocides in history have been recognized under the 1948 legal definition: the [Cambodian genocide](/wiki/Cambodian_genocide "Cambodian genocide"), the [Rwandan genocide](/wiki/Rwandan_genocide "Rwandan genocide"), and the [Srebrenica massacre](/wiki/Srebrenica_massacre "Srebrenica massacre").[[6]](#cite_note-Samuel_2023-7)

According to Ernesto Verdeja, associate professor of political science and peace studies at the University of Notre Dame, there are three ways to conceptualize genocide other than the legal definition: in academic social science, in international politics and policy, and in colloquial public usage. The academic social science approach does not require proof of intent,[[6]](#cite_note-Samuel_2023-7) and social scientists often define genocide more broadly.[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurga2023-8) The international politics and policy definition centres around prevention policy and intervention and may actually mean "large-scale violence against civilians" when used by governments and international organizations. Lastly, Verdeja says the way the general public colloquially uses "genocide" is usually "as a stand-in term for the greatest evils".[[6]](#cite_note-Samuel_2023-7)

This list includes all events which have been classified as [genocide](/wiki/Genocide "Genocide") by significant scholarship. As there are varying [definitions of genocide](/wiki/Definitions_of_genocide "Definitions of genocide"), this list includes events around which there is ongoing scholarly debate over their classification as *genocide* and is not a list of only events which have a scholarly consensus to recognize them as genocide. This list excludes [mass killings](/wiki/Mass_killing "Mass killing") which have not been explicitly defined as genocidal.[[a]](#cite_note-2)

Definitions
-----------

Main article: [Genocide definitions](/wiki/Genocide_definitions "Genocide definitions")

Scholarship varies on the [definition of genocide](/wiki/Genocide_definitions "Genocide definitions") employed when analysing whether events are genocidal in nature.[[2]](#cite_note-3) The United Nations [Genocide Convention](/wiki/Genocide_Convention "Genocide Convention"), not always employed, defines genocide as "any of the following acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group, as such: killing members of the group; causing serious bodily or mental harm to members of the group; deliberately inflicting on the group conditions of life calculated to bring about its physical destruction in whole or in part; imposing measures intended to prevent births within the group; [and] forcibly transferring children of the group to another group".[[3]](#cite_note-4) This and other definitions are generally regarded by the majority of genocide scholars to have an "[intent to destroy](/wiki/Genocidal_intent "Genocidal intent")" as a requirement for any act to be labelled genocide; there is also growing agreement on the inclusion of the physical destruction criterion.[[4]](#cite_note-AdamJones2024-5) Writing in 1998, professors of sociology Kurt Jonassohn and Karin Björnson stated that the Genocide Convention was a legal instrument resulting from a diplomatic compromise; the wording of the treaty is not intended to be a definition suitable as a research tool, and although it is used for this purpose, as it has an international legal credibility that others lack, other definitions have also been postulated. Jonassohn and Björnson go on to say that for various reasons, none of these alternative definitions have gained widespread support.[[5]](#cite_note-6)

Three genocides in history have been recognized under the 1948 legal definition: the [Cambodian genocide](/wiki/Cambodian_genocide "Cambodian genocide"), the [Rwandan genocide](/wiki/Rwandan_genocide "Rwandan genocide"), and the [Srebrenica massacre](/wiki/Srebrenica_massacre "Srebrenica massacre").[[6]](#cite_note-Samuel_2023-7)

According to Ernesto Verdeja, associate professor of political science and peace studies at the University of Notre Dame, there are three ways to conceptualize genocide other than the legal definition: in academic social science, in international politics and policy, and in colloquial public usage. The academic social science approach does not require proof of intent,[[6]](#cite_note-Samuel_2023-7) and social scientists often define genocide more broadly.[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurga2023-8) The international politics and policy definition centres around prevention policy and intervention and may actually mean "large-scale violence against civilians" when used by governments and international organizations. Lastly, Verdeja says the way the general public colloquially uses "genocide" is usually "as a stand-in term for the greatest evils".[[6]](#cite_note-Samuel_2023-7)

The Holodomor was part of the wider [Soviet famine of 1930–1933](/wiki/Soviet_famine_of_1930%E2%80%931933 "Soviet famine of 1930–1933") which affected the major [grain-producing](/wiki/Agriculture "Agriculture") areas of the [Soviet Union](/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union").  While scholars are in consensus that the [cause of the famine](/wiki/Causes_of_the_Holodomor "Causes of the Holodomor") was man-made,[[247]](#cite_note-254) [whether or not the Holodomor was intentional](/wiki/Holodomor_genocide_question "Holodomor genocide question") and therefore constitutes a [genocide](/wiki/Genocide "Genocide") under the [Genocide Convention](/wiki/Genocide_Convention "Genocide Convention") is debated by scholars.[[248]](#cite_note-255)[[249]](#cite_note-256) | | 10% of Ukraine's population[[250]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEllman2007-257) Over 35% of [Ukrainians in Kazakhstan](/wiki/Ukrainians_in_Kazakhstan "Ukrainians in Kazakhstan")[[251]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOhayon2016-258) | | | |

| The Holocaust was the [genocide](/wiki/Genocide "Genocide") of [European Jews](/wiki/History_of_the_Jews_in_Europe "History of the Jews in Europe") during [World War II](/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"). Between 1941 and 1945, [Nazi Germany](/wiki/Nazi_Germany "Nazi Germany") and [its collaborators](/wiki/Collaboration_with_Nazi_Germany_and_Fascist_Italy "Collaboration with Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy") systematically murdered some [six million Jews](/wiki/Holocaust_victims "Holocaust victims") across [German-occupied Europe](/wiki/German-occupied_Europe "German-occupied Europe"), around two-thirds of Europe's Jewish population.[[197]](#cite_note-202)[[198]](#cite_note-203)[[199]](#cite_note-204) Nearly one and half million were killed in just 100 days from late July to early November 1942.[[200]](#cite_note-205) The murders were carried out primarily through mass shootings and poison gas in [extermination camps](/wiki/Extermination_camp "Extermination camp").[[201]](#cite_note-HoloList-206) Separate Nazi persecutions killed a similar or larger number of non-Jewish civilians and POWs; the term *Holocaust* is sometimes used to refer to the persecution of these [other groups](/wiki/Holocaust_victims "Holocaust victims"). The Holocaust is considered to be the single largest genocide in history.[[202]](#cite_note-207)[[203]](#cite_note-208) | | Around 2/3 of the [Jewish population of Europe](/wiki/History_of_the_Jews_in_Europe "History of the Jews in Europe").[[204]](#cite_note-209)[[205]](#cite_note-210) | | | |

This list includes all events which have been classified as [genocide](/wiki/Genocide "Genocide") by significant scholarship. As there are varying [definitions of genocide](/wiki/Definitions_of_genocide "Definitions of genocide"), this list includes events around which there is ongoing scholarly debate over their classification as *genocide* and is not a list of only events which have a scholarly consensus to recognize them as genocide. This list excludes [mass killings](/wiki/Mass_killing "Mass killing") which have not been explicitly defined as genocidal.[[a]](#cite_note-2)

Definitions
-----------

Main article: [Genocide definitions](/wiki/Genocide_definitions "Genocide definitions")

Scholarship varies on the [definition of genocide](/wiki/Genocide_definitions "Genocide definitions") employed when analysing whether events are genocidal in nature.[[2]](#cite_note-3) The United Nations [Genocide Convention](/wiki/Genocide_Convention "Genocide Convention"), not always employed, defines genocide as "any of the following acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group, as such: killing members of the group; causing serious bodily or mental harm to members of the group; deliberately inflicting on the group conditions of life calculated to bring about its physical destruction in whole or in part; imposing measures intended to prevent births within the group; [and] forcibly transferring children of the group to another group".[[3]](#cite_note-4) This and other definitions are generally regarded by the majority of genocide scholars to have an "[intent to destroy](/wiki/Genocidal_intent "Genocidal intent")" as a requirement for any act to be labelled genocide; there is also growing agreement on the inclusion of the physical destruction criterion.[[4]](#cite_note-AdamJones2024-5) Writing in 1998, professors of sociology Kurt Jonassohn and Karin Björnson stated that the Genocide Convention was a legal instrument resulting from a diplomatic compromise; the wording of the treaty is not intended to be a definition suitable as a research tool, and although it is used for this purpose, as it has an international legal credibility that others lack, other definitions have also been postulated. Jonassohn and Björnson go on to say that for various reasons, none of these alternative definitions have gained widespread support.[[5]](#cite_note-6)

Three genocides in history have been recognized under the 1948 legal definition: the [Cambodian genocide](/wiki/Cambodian_genocide "Cambodian genocide"), the [Rwandan genocide](/wiki/Rwandan_genocide "Rwandan genocide"), and the [Srebrenica massacre](/wiki/Srebrenica_massacre "Srebrenica massacre").[[6]](#cite_note-Samuel_2023-7)

According to Ernesto Verdeja, associate professor of political science and peace studies at the University of Notre Dame, there are three ways to conceptualize genocide other than the legal definition: in academic social science, in international politics and policy, and in colloquial public usage. The academic social science approach does not require proof of intent,[[6]](#cite_note-Samuel_2023-7) and social scientists often define genocide more broadly.[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurga2023-8) The international politics and policy definition centres around prevention policy and intervention and may actually mean "large-scale violence against civilians" when used by governments and international organizations. Lastly, Verdeja says the way the general public colloquially uses "genocide" is usually "as a stand-in term for the greatest evils".[[6]](#cite_note-Samuel_2023-7)
